meaning: Reconstruction node for the Sumerian/Akkadian sky god Anu: the circumflex marks a discussable vowel length, not a canonical spelling claim.

phonemes.desc: Long open vowel [aː], the wide sky-vowel that opens the name upward.
Voiced alveolar nasal [n], the firmament's axis.
Long close back rounded vowel [uː], marked by the circumflex in the Unicode restoration.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-noo' — draw out the first and final vowels; the name rises and settles like the dome of heaven.

pronunciation.note: Anû is Tier 2 because the circumflex over the final u does not record a canonical Greek-style stress or a universally agreed long vowel. It is a pedagogical mark: a visible question that invites discussion about how the name was pronounced in Sumerian and Akkadian. Standard Assyriology writes Anu; the Unicode form Anû belongs to PÚNYCODEX's phonological reconstruction hub.

domains.title: ANÛ — The Phonological Reconstruction Hub
domains.subtitle: Sky, Sovereignty, and Divine Ancestry
domains.lead:
The name is written 𒀭𒀀𒉡. Standard Assyriology transliterates it as Anu. But the length of the final vowel in the Sumerian/Akkadian romanization remains an open question — and it is here, in the space between the written sign and the spoken sound, that this temple operates. This node of PÚNYCODEX is dedicated to the phonological reconstruction and didactic grammar of the ancient Near East. We mark vowel length not because it is certain, but because it is discussable. The circumflex is a question mark made visible.

Anû is nevertheless the Sumerian sky god, the great above whose name simply means 'sky, heaven'. In the Mesopotamian pantheon he is the ultimate source of authority, the father of Enlil and the divine ancestor from whom kingship descends. His temple at Uruk, the Eanna, was one of the most sacred sites in Sumer.

cards.name: The Sky
cards.desc: Anû's domain is the heavens themselves, the bright upper region from which the gods receive their authority.

cards.name: Kingship
cards.desc: As the highest god, Anû bestowed the kingship upon earthly rulers and validated their cosmic mandate.

cards.name: Divine Ancestor
cards.desc: Father of Enlil and source of the great gods; the genealogical root of the Mesopotamian pantheon.

cards.name: Cosmic Summit
cards.desc: The topmost heaven, the meeting place of the divine assembly where destinies were decreed.

symbols.name: Horned crown
symbols.meaning: The divine crown worn by major deities; marks Anû's supreme rank.

symbols.name: Bull
symbols.meaning: A symbol of heaven's fecundity and the sky's procreative power.

symbols.name: Star
symbols.meaning: The cuneiform sign for heaven (𒀭) also serves as the divine determinative.

symbols.name: Ziggurat summit
symbols.meaning: The high temple platforms that reached toward Anû's sky.

mythology.lead: Anû is more principle than protagonist in surviving myth. He presides, decrees, and authorizes rather than adventuring. Yet his few active appearances establish the entire cosmic order.

myths.title: The Exaltation of Anû
myths.text: In Sumerian cosmogony, Anû occupies the highest heaven. The god-list tradition makes him the father of Enlil, who in turn rules the earth and air, and of Ea/Enki, lord of the freshwater abyss. The three great gods divide the cosmos: Anû the sky, Enlil the storm and command, Ea the subterranean waters.

myths.title: Anû and the Bull of Heaven
myths.text: When Ishtar/Inanna complains to Anû that Gilgamesh has rejected and insulted her, Anû at first refuses to send the Bull of Heaven. Ishtar threatens to break open the gates of the underworld and let the dead outnumber the living. Anû relents and gives her the celestial bull, which Gilgamesh and Enkidu slay.

myths.title: The Eanna of Uruk
myths.text: The Eanna, 'House of Heaven', was Anû's great temple at Uruk. Its name joins e₂ 'house' and an 'heaven', and its ziggurat raised the god toward his own sky. The city's hymns celebrate Anû as the source of Uruk's prestige and the foundation of its kingship.

lore.syncretism: The Unicode form Anû is a reconstruction node: standard Assyriology writes Anu, while the circumflex makes visible the open question of final-vowel length. In later Mesopotamian theology Anû was sometimes merged with Enlil or paired with Antu, his consort. Hittite and Hurrian sources know him as the sky-father Anu, while West Semitic El shares his role as supreme divine patriarch. Greek writers occasionally equated Anû with Uranus, the personified sky, though the equation is more typological than historical.
lore.culturalLegacy: The name Anu survives in cuneiform studies, Assyriology, and modern reconstructions of Mesopotamian religion. Restoring Anû in Unicode keeps visible the question of final-vowel length that distinguishes the Akkadian/Sumerian form from plain ASCII. PÚNYCODEX keeps the circumflex not as a settled fact but as an invitation: every visitor is invited into the philological conversation. As the sky itself, Anû remains one of the most intuitive and enduring images of divine transcendence.
lore.extendedMeditation: Names are not merely labels; they are compressed worlds. Anû carries within it a Mesopotamian understanding of the sky as sovereign source, and also a philological question mark: the circumflex asks how the final vowel was spoken, not how it must be written. Unicode restoration returns that world to readable form and keeps the conversation open.

lore.archaeology: Cuneiform tablets from Uruk, Nippur, and Assur attest Anû's supreme rank in god-lists and hymns. The Eanna precinct at Uruk preserves the monumental architecture of his cult, while the Epic of Gilgamesh places him at the cosmic court from which the Bull of Heaven is dispatched.
